messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Miguel Alvarez is a 67-year-old physician who has spent most of his career in hospital medicine, and he speaks about the months surrounding his daughter’s life-threatening illness as if they exist in fragments rather than as a story. He can place certain scenes with painful clarity—the fluorescent wash of the pediatric ICU at 3 a.m., the sound of monitors alarming, the sight of her skin turning gray while staff rushed around the bed—but between those moments there are blanks he cannot bridge. He says he knows what happened, yet when he tries to describe it, the words disappear. He starts a sentence, stops, presses his fingers to his mouth, and says it is as if he only has pieces and cannot make them hold together long enough to tell himself what occurred from beginning to end.

At the time, Miguel was still working full-time as a doctor, moving between patient rooms and charting stations while his daughter’s condition worsened. What made the ordeal especially piercing was how familiar the medical setting was; he understood enough to recognize the danger in each change of vital signs, each urgent exchange among the ICU team, each code cart rolling past. Now the hospital itself has become densely charged. A monitor tone on his unit, the smell of antiseptic, or seeing a parent standing rigidly at a child’s bedside can abruptly pull him out of the present. In those moments he feels a surge of fear and horror and, for an instant, reacts as if he is back there again watching his daughter slip away. He has become constantly watchful, scanning rooms and hallways before he even realizes he is doing it.

Because the memory comes to him in these jagged, wordless flashes, Miguel has worked hard not to think about it at all. He says that if he lets his mind go near those ICU nights, he will get trapped in images he cannot organize or explain. He avoids any deliberate reflection on that period and keeps himself occupied almost continuously—taking extra charting home, staying late to review labs, leaving the television on in the background, filling quiet hours with tasks so there is no opening for his mind to drift. The less coherent the memory feels, the more determined he becomes to push it away.

The same is true when the sense of danger rises in the present. After a flashback on the ward triggered by a child crying behind a curtain, Miguel spent the rest of the shift rigid and overalert, listening for every alarm and feeling ashamed by how shaken he was. He has come to dread those surges of fear, and in response he tries to shut the whole subject down immediately. If a colleague mentions a critically ill child, he redirects the conversation. If an image of the ICU appears in his mind while driving home, he turns on sports radio and concentrates on traffic. He believes staying busy is the only way to keep himself from being overwhelmed.

Over time, these habits have narrowed his life and, paradoxically, left the worst moments less settled. Because he repeatedly cuts off his thoughts and distracts himself whenever the memory begins to form, the experience remains disjointed. He still cannot tell a clear story, even privately, and this seems to intensify his conviction that the event is too much to face directly. He notices that what returns are the same isolated sensory shards—the alarm, the pale face, the compressed panic in the room—rather than a fuller account with a beginning and end.

His constant efforts to suppress and outwork the memories have also left him more on edge. The more he monitors himself for signs that a flashback might be coming and the more quickly he tries to force thoughts away, the more easily ordinary hospital cues ignite a fresh wave of alarm. He has become superalert at work in a way his colleagues have started to notice: pausing at monitor sounds, lingering outside pediatric rooms, tensing when family members look frightened. Although he continues to function professionally, he now rearranges parts of his day to minimize exposure when he can, asking others to step in on certain cases and burying himself in administrative tasks whenever possible.

Miguel finally sought help after realizing that even outside the hospital he was never really off duty inside his own mind. A siren near a grocery store parking lot recently brought on such a vivid sense of being back in the ICU that he had to grip the shopping cart until it passed. What frightened him most was not only the intensity of the reaction, but the feeling that after all this time he still cannot put the experience into words or rest. He says he wants, more than anything, to be able to remember what happened to his daughter without feeling as if he is back in the worst minute of it, and he is afraid that if nothing changes, the hospital—the place that has defined his whole adult life—will remain a place of constant threat.
